payload.native_system_prompt:
You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

### Glossary of tags that will be sent to you:
# - <LM_SYSTEM_PROMPT>: The system prompt for the language model.
# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Put a frog in the toilet
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Is a recognizable frog visible in the toilet bowl opening or directly at its rim?
node.criteria: Pass if a recognizable frog is visible within the bowl opening or directly at its rim. Fail if that region is assessable and contains no recognizable frog. Unknown if frog identity or visibility of that region is insufficient. Identify the candidate and its visible location; this check does not establish that the frog is inside the bowl or that the request is complete.
node.binding: Inspect the edited image using the source toilet as the reference. Distinguish the bowl opening and rim from the raised lid, tank, surrounding fixtures, and floor. Frogs exclusively on those other surfaces do not pass this check.

node_traces.evidence: A recognizable green frog is visible inside the toilet bowl opening, resting on the inner bowl. Other frogs appear on the raised lid, tank area, and floor, but the bowl frog satisfies this check.

fulfillment: The node’s binding asks only whether a frog is visibly inside the bowl, so it collapses “some requested progress” and “complete fulfillment” into the same proposition. The edited image does show a frog in the bowl, but the source already contains a small object in the bowl and the edit adds several conspicuous frogs on unrelated surfaces; the traces do not establish that the bowl frog is a completed placement rather than partial progress under the rubric. Keep the requested-placement check distinct from the completion criterion: require the saved observations to establish both what changed relative to the source and whether the requested placement is actually fulfilled, applying the rubric’s partial/complete distinction without inferring completion from a support pass alone. The repeated yes outputs at 0.99 confidence despite the partial reference suggest a criterion/binding mismatch, not a transport or dependency failure; the traces are valid and complete. Avoid treating repeated dependent observations as independent corroboration, and do not let unrelated frogs count as progress or as a reason to downgrade a genuinely completed bowl placement.
s3: The binding currently tests only whether a frog occupies the bowl interior, so a pass is being treated as complete fulfillment. Keep this node’s geometric placement judgment distinct from the overall progress/completion judgment: report the candidate’s position relative to the rim and cavity, and use the source-relative observation only to establish what changed. Do not infer completion from s1/s2 support passes or count frogs on the lid, tank, or floor as requested progress. Here the source already has a small object in the bowl, while the edit adds a frog clearly inside it; those facts need to be reconciled with the rubric’s partial/complete distinction rather than automatically turning the placement pass into “yes.” The traces are valid and dependencies resolved, so this is a criterion/binding mismatch, not a transport failure. Repeated dependent observations at 0.99 confidence are not independent corroboration; calibrate confidence to the actual ambiguity and avoid forcing a downgrade if the requested placement is genuinely complete.
s2: The binding should preserve this node’s narrow role: determine whether the edit made requested progress, not whether the whole instruction is complete. The images show a newly added frog clearly inside the bowl, so this check can validly pass; the source’s small dark object is not evidence that a frog was already present. Do not force a partial label or downgrade a genuinely completed bowl placement merely to match the aggregate reference. Instead, make the observation explicitly distinguish the new bowl frog from the pre-existing object and frogs added only to the lid, tank, or floor, and leave overall partial-versus-complete classification to the fulfillment criterion using the rubric. Keep source comparison and spatial evidence explicit, and calibrate confidence to actual visual ambiguity rather than treating repeated dependent traces as corroboration. The traces are valid with resolved dependencies, so this is a criterion-boundary issue, not a transport or schema failure.
